She together with Isolde spent nearly all their time outside, taking immense pleasure in every joy provided by Linger Lane, the Nymph’s Well, Reedmere, and Victoria Island. Nell’s wandering habits met with no opposition from Thirza. Early in the vacation, during an afternoon visit to a patient's home, Nell encountered the Tullyvale doctor who had previously attended Posy Fay on the night she suffered from croup; he scrutinized Nell intently, pursed his lips, shook his head, and dispatched a message to Thirza Abernethy through a third party. The message ran:
passages.v01:c31:p0010: When Miss Thorne returned to Brierley school, she discovered that every one of her students was keen to resume studying. The Regent’s class in particular prepared themselves for the battle, since at the conclusion of the approaching year, cast like a faint shadow across their road even now, towered that ominous event called “the Entrance,” a prospect that caused the hearts of each single person to plunge into their boots. What if they failed? It was a question that would torment Nell during her conscious moments throughout that winter, not excepting Sunday afternoons, driving out nearly every ethical and religious matter. Whenever Nell suffered nightmares, she saw herself gazing wretchedly at Entrance examination pass lists that displayed Hugh Carrow’s name triumphantly at the head and lacked hers altogether.

Thirza adored the girl no less than she had adored the child, yet she recognized a strange, mournful feeling of bereavement. Although she had frequently given public recitations, an assembly like this had never confronted her before, and her energies were totally paralyzed by the vision of it. Every element—the lines of women wearing evening gowns, the discerning expressions, the entire environment of affluence and refinement surrounding her—proved exceedingly unfamiliar, dazzling, and disorienting. unit: At school, Hugh silently competes with Nell while ignoring her, leaving her to regret her past harshness as the term ends. Miss Thorne reassures the class that she will return next year, prompting Nell to happily lock away her books for summer vacation. Later, Agatha Sowerby visits Thirza at Grey Shutters and compliments Nell's growth and grace despite her initial misgivings.

passages.v01:c30:p0025: Ever since that afternoon beside the water when she had declined to hear his entreaty for pardon, Hugh, except for the previously mentioned firm competition, had shown not the slightest acknowledgment that Nell Harcourt existed. He conversed and joked with the remaining maidens, traded volumes and riddles with them, debated studies and schemes, and occasionally accompanied one or another of them back from religious service or the Debating Club. Yet he entirely disregarded Nell Harcourt, and Nell discovered that being disregarded is far from agreeable. It availed her nothing to assure herself with a flip of her hair that it mattered not to her. Far within her erratic, female young spirit, she was aware that it truly mattered, and that were she granted a second opportunity at the Lake of Glassy Waters, her reply would be altogether altered. Quite suddenly, as it appeared, and to her hidden distress, she realized that the former ill will she had harbored toward him had vanished—vanished precisely when its supportive strength was most required. She strove to no purpose as she summoned back each event and feeling of that unforgettable event, trying to experience the former comforting wrath. That afternoon beside the water had seen its final brief flare. Nell came to understand that she had granted pardon and put it out of mind unawares. Nevertheless, the time had passed.
passages.v01:c30:p0032: “Indeed, I believe I shall,” Miss Thorne remarked. “I considered accepting a position at a different school, yet my decision is to return to Brierley.
